notes.meaning: Jesus returned to His hometown of Nazareth, bringing His disciples along with Him. He had faced hostility there earlier, yet He returned to offer His own people another opportunity to hear God's truth. True disciples follow their Master wherever He leads, even into unwelcoming places.

On the Sabbath, Jesus taught in the local synagogue, the Jewish meeting place for worship and reading Scripture. The listeners were stunned by the depth of His wisdom and the reports of His miracles. Instead of receiving Him, their astonishment turned to envy, and they began questioning how an ordinary neighbor could have such authority.

The villagers looked down on Jesus because they knew Him as their local carpenter, an artisan who worked with wood. They were familiar with His mother Mary and His brothers and sisters, and this ordinary background offended them. Because they thought they knew everything about Him, they stumbled and refused to believe.

differ.view: Believe the brothers and sisters listed here were the biological children of Joseph and Mary, born after the virgin birth of Jesus.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Teaches that Mary remained a virgin her whole life, meaning the 'brothers' and 'sisters' were close relatives or cousins rather than children of Mary.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Holds that these siblings were children of Joseph from an earlier marriage before he was betrothed to Mary.

notes.meaning: Jesus replied with a common proverb, pointing out that God's messengers are usually welcomed everywhere except by their closest friends, relatives, and neighbors. People often struggle to respect spiritual authority in someone they watched grow up. Jesus quietly bore this painful rejection as part of His earthly path.

Jesus did not perform major miracles in Nazareth because the people had shut their hearts in stubborn unbelief. It was not that His divine strength failed, but doing mighty signs among those who hardened themselves went against God's wise plan. Even amidst their coldness, His compassion led Him to lay hands on a few sick people and heal them.

Jesus was amazed at how deeply their unbelief ran, especially among those who had the best chance to know Him. In His genuine human nature, He felt the sadness and surprise of seeing people reject God's grace. He then moved on from Nazareth, traveling through the surrounding villages to teach the people.

Jesus gathered the twelve apostles and sent them out on their first preaching tour in pairs. Traveling two by two provided companionship, mutual encouragement, and the two witnesses required by Jewish law. He also shared His own authority with them to cast out evil spirits.

Jesus commanded the disciples to travel light, taking only a walking staff and sandals, while leaving behind extra bread, travel bags, money, and spare tunics. They were to rely completely on God to supply their daily food and shelter through the kindness of the people they served. By traveling without extra belongings, they stayed focused and moved quickly without worldly entanglements.

The apostles were instructed to remain in the first home that welcomed them until they finished their work in that town. They were not to move around looking for better food or finer lodging, which would hurt their hosts' feelings. Being content with simple hospitality kept their eyes on their spiritual mission.

If any town refused to welcome the apostles or listen to their message, they were to shake the dust off their feet as they walked away. This dramatic Jewish custom served as a public warning that the town had rejected God's offer of salvation and would face His judgment. The apostles could move on with a clear conscience, knowing they had done their part.

The disciples went out preaching that everyone needed to repent, meaning to turn away from sin and return to God. This call to a changed heart and reformed life was the very message John the Baptist and Jesus had been preaching. Real faith always begins with turning from evil to follow God.

The apostles drove out many demons and healed large numbers of sick people by anointing them with olive oil. The oil was used as a visible sign of God's soothing care and miraculous healing touch. These mighty works proved that their message came from heaven and that God's kingdom was breaking into the world.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Considers this anointing by the apostles to be an early sign and foreshadowing of the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick.

notes.meaning: News of the apostles' successful preaching tour reached King Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee. Because Jesus' name was now known everywhere, Herod became convinced that John the Baptist had risen from the dead and was working these miracles. A guilty conscience made the king imagine that the prophet he put to death had returned with supernatural power.

Other people tried to explain Jesus by saying He was the prophet Elijah, who was expected to return before the Messiah, or one of the ancient prophets sent back to Israel. Although they recognized that God was at work, they still failed to grasp that Jesus was the promised Christ. Human opinions often fall short of the full truth about who Jesus is.

Herod ignored the other explanations and insisted that Jesus was John, the very prophet he had beheaded. His terrible memory of the execution haunted him day and night. Unconfessed sin often fills the human heart with terror and dread.

Mark explains how Herod had earlier sent soldiers to arrest John and lock him up in the fortress of Machaerus. Herod did this to please Herodias, whom he had unlawfully taken from his half-brother Philip to make his own wife. Sinful relationships often push people to silence God's messengers.

John had repeatedly warned Herod that taking his brother's living wife broke the clear law of God. John showed tremendous courage by confronting a dangerous monarch about his private moral failure. God's moral law applies to earthly rulers just as strictly as to everyday people.

Herodias hated John for calling out her sin and nursed a bitter grudge against him. She wanted to execute him immediately, but she could not do so because Herod prevented her. Unchecked pride and guilt can quickly turn into murderous hatred toward those who speak the truth.

Herod shielded John from his wife because he respected him as an upright and holy servant of God. Even though John's preaching deeply troubled Herod's conscience, the ruler still enjoyed listening to him speak. Herod liked good preaching, but he was unwilling to turn away from the favorite sins that ruled his life.

Herodias finally found her opportunity when Herod threw a grand birthday banquet for his court officials, military commanders, and the leading men of Galilee. The gathering was full of luxury, wine, and political show. This secular feast provided the perfect setting for Herodias to spring her deadly trap.

Herodias sent her young daughter into the banquet hall to dance for the king and his drunken guests. Her performance delighted Herod and the men at his table so much that he made a wild and reckless promise, telling her she could ask for whatever she wanted.

Herod went further by binding his offer with a formal oath, swearing to give the girl anything she requested up to half of his kingdom. This boastful royal phrase showed how completely pride and wine had destroyed his judgment. Foolish promises made in haste often lead to terrible heartbreak.

The girl stepped out of the hall to consult her mother about what she should request. Herodias did not hesitate for a moment, instructing her daughter to ask for the head of John the Baptist. Her instant answer revealed that she had planned all along to use this occasion to silence God's prophet.

The girl rushed back to the king right away to make her gruesome demand before his reckless mood could fade. She insisted that John's head be brought to her immediately on a large platter. Cruelty had taken root in her young heart under the influence of her bitter mother.

Herod was filled with deep grief because he knew John was an innocent and holy man. Even so, cowardly pride and fear of being mocked by his banquet guests kept him from refusing her request. He chose to commit a monstrous crime rather than face public embarrassment by breaking a rash vow.

The king immediately dispatched an executioner from his personal bodyguard to carry out the order. The soldier went into the dark prison and cut off the head of the prophet. John died as a faithful martyr, giving up his earthly life rather than compromising God's truth.

The guard brought John's head into the hall on a platter and gave it to the girl, who carried it directly to her mother. Herodias seemed to win her bitter victory, but she could not silence the voice of God. While wicked people may shed innocent blood, God treasures the life of His faithful servants and will bring all deeds to judgment.
